deep.reconstruction:
Overview. The page is a scratch sheet. Its central computation tests whether a power series with coefficients in Q(ε) can be factored into a product of triple-product type. Here ε = exp(2πi/5) is a primitive fifth root of unity. The surrounding jottings and the next page, with products split as P(...)+Q(...) and factors over residue classes mod 5, place this in Gauss's work on theta-product dissections modulo 5.

(1) Top line: (1 + 2e^{-π/α} + ...) = √a. This is the theta series θ3(q) = 1 + 2q + 2q^4 + 2q^9 + ... at q = e^{-π/α}, set equal to √a. It belongs to Gauss's AGM / lemniscatic theta circle, where θ3(q)^2 relates to the AGM and complete elliptic integrals. It is only a reminder; nothing is derived from it.

(2) The identity 2/(1+√5) = (√5-1)/2 (golden-ratio reciprocal).

(3) A first trial series: 1 + ½(√5-1)x + ½(√5-1)x^4 + ½(√5-1)x^5 + ...

(4) It is rewritten via ε + ε^4 = 2cos(2π/5) = (√5-1)/2 =: c. The x^5 coefficient is corrected to 2 - ε - ε^4 = 2 - c = (5-√5)/2. This explains the side computations √5 - 1 = 2ε + 2ε^4, 1 + 2ε + 2ε^4 (= √5, the quadratic Gauss sum mod 5), 2√5/(1+√5) and (5-√5)/2 (= 2 - c).

The series is S = 1 + c x + c x^4 + (2-c) x^5 + c x^9 + ...

(5) Successive division ('1+εx | ...' means quotient after dividing by 1+εx).

(a) S/(1+εx) = 1 + ε^4 x - x^2 + ε x^3 + (ε - ε^2 + ε^4) x^4 + (1 - ε - ε^2 + ε^3 - ε^4) x^5 + ... (I verified each coefficient.)

(b) Dividing that by (1+ε^4 x) gives 1 - x^2 + (ε+ε^4) x^3 - (1 - ε + ε^2 + ε^3 - ε^4) x^4 + t5 x^5. Gauss writes t5 = -2ε^2 + 2ε^3.

(c) Dividing by (1-x^2) gives 1 + (ε+ε^4) x^3 + 2(ε+ε^4) x^4 + ..., where Gauss stops.

The point is to strip off factors (1+εx)(1+ε^4x)(1-x^2)... and see whether the next factor is (1+εx^3)(1+ε^4x^3) = 1 + c x^3 + x^6. The result 1 + c x^3 + 2c x^4 + ... shows S is NOT simply the triple product with z = ε. In my simplification, using ε^2 + ε^3 = -1 - c and c^2 = 1 - c, the x^4 coefficient in (b) equals 2c.

(6) Right-hand jottings. '1+εx · 1+ε^4x | (1+x^5)/(1+x)' records that (1+εx)(1+ε^4x) is a factor of (1+x^5)/(1+x) = ∏_{k=1}^4 (1+ε^k x). Likewise (1+x^15)/(1+x^3) and (1+x^20)/(1+x^4) are products ∏_{k=1}^4 (1+ε^k x^n) for n = 3, 4. Gauss is thus thinking of products ∏_n (1+x^{5n})/(1+x^n), which split over the conjugate pairs {ε, ε^4} and {ε^2, ε^3}. The entry '|1-xx|^2' appears to be a squared (1-x^2) factor (reading mine).

(7) Rotated lower-left jottings (partly illegible). They contain products of factors (1±x^n) with n in residue classes mod 5, e.g. n = 1, 4, 6, 9, 11, 14, 19 (n ≡ ±1 mod 5), and quotients over (1+x)^4. There is also the progression 1, 4, 7, 10, 13, 16 and fragmentary equations of the form ∏(1-x^2y...)... = ..., with an integral sign. These anticipate the next page's P/Q dissections of (1+xy)(1-x^3y)(1-x^7/y)(1+x^9/y)....

(8) Lower-right fraction arithmetic. This includes -4/6 + 10/6 - 4/6 and entries 2/12, 8/24, -10/12 + 40/24, -20/24. It is coefficient scratch-work whose purpose I cannot determine with certainty.
errors: In the division by (1+ε^4x), the x^5 coefficient of the quotient is 0, not -2ε^2 + 2ε^3. Check: with T(1 + c x + x^2) = S, t5 = (2-c) - c·t4 - t3 = 2 - c - 2c^2 - c = 0 using c^2 = 1 - c. Gauss's value is purely imaginary and so cannot arise in a product of conjugate pairs with real result. He does not carry the x^5 term into the next line, so the slip has no consequence on the page.
The first trial series has x^5 coefficient ½(√5-1). It is superseded in the next line by 2 - ε - ε^4 = (5-√5)/2, so the first version was a guess later corrected.

Correct on the page: 2/(1+√5) = (√5-1)/2, √5 - 1 = 2ε + 2ε^4, 1 + 2ε + 2ε^4 = √5, 2√5/(1+√5) = (5-√5)/2, and all coefficients of the first quotient and the x^0..x^4 coefficients of the second. The third quotient is also correct through x^4; its x^5 term would be c.

results.what: 1 + 2e^{-π/α} + 2e^{-4π/α} + ... = √a (theta series tied to an AGM-type quantity)
results.modern_name: Jacobi theta function θ3 and its relation to the AGM / complete elliptic integral
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (1790s-1800, Nachlass); Jacobi (1829) in published form

results.what: ε + ε^4 = (√5-1)/2 and 1 + 2ε + 2ε^4 = √5 for ε a primitive 5th root of unity
results.modern_name: Quadratic Gauss sum mod 5 / Gaussian periods (cyclotomy)

results.what: (1+x^5)/(1+x) = ∏_{k=1}^4 (1+ε^k x), and similarly for x^3, x^4; used to split products ∏(1+x^{5n})/(1+x^n) into conjugate-pair factors
results.modern_name: Cyclotomic factorization of q-products; mod-5 dissection of infinite products
results.usually_credited_to: Classical (Gauss/Jacobi); systematic mod-5 dissections later in Ramanujan and Rogers

results.what: Trial factorization by power-series division of S = 1 + c x + c x^4 + (2-c)x^5 + ... into (1+εx)(1+ε^4x)(1-x^2)·(1 + c x^3 + 2c x^4 + ...)
results.modern_name: Testing a Jacobi triple-product form with root-of-unity argument (theta products at z = ε)

deep.surprise_reason: This is exploratory scratch-work: theta series, a quadratic Gauss sum mod 5 and fifth-root-of-unity factorizations of q-products. All lie within topics well documented as Gauss's (Disquisitiones, theta/AGM Nachlass, triple product). The mod-5 product dissections hinted at here and on the next page touch territory later associated with Rogers–Ramanujan, but this page contains no identity of that kind. The main computation ends in a non-factorization, plus a minor slip.

checkable.sympy: x=symbols('x'); c=(sqrt(5)-1)/2; S=1+c*x+c*x**4+(2-c)*x**5; T=series(S/(1+c*x+x**2),x,0,6).removeO(); [simplify(T.coeff(x,k)) for k in range(6)]
checkable.asserts: S/((1+εx)(1+ε^4x)) = 1 - x^2 + c x^3 + 2c x^4 + 0·x^5 + O(x^6); the x^5 coefficient is 0, not Gauss's -2ε^2 + 2ε^3

checkable.sympy: x=symbols('x'); e=exp(2*pi*I/5); c=e+e**4; S=1+c*x+c*x**4+(2-c)*x**5; Q=series(S/(1+e*x),x,0,6).removeO(); [simplify(expand_complex(Q.coeff(x,k)-v)) for k,v in enumerate([1,e**4,-1,e,e-e**2+e**4,1-e-e**2+e**3-e**4])]
checkable.asserts: First quotient S/(1+εx) matches Gauss's coefficients through x^5 (all differences zero)

checkable.sympy: x=symbols('x'); c=(sqrt(5)-1)/2; T=1-x**2+c*x**3+2*c*x**4; U=series(T/(1-x**2),x,0,5).removeO(); [simplify(U.coeff(x,k)) for k in range(5)]
checkable.asserts: Third division: quotient is 1 + c x^3 + 2c x^4 + ..., as written

transcription_corrections: In the second division line the x^4 coefficient reads -(1-ε+εε+ε^3-ε^4); the obscured symbol before ε^4 is a minus sign. This value equals 2(ε+ε^4).
'(1+x^{15})/(1+x^3)' is correct as read; it parallels (1+x^5)/(1+x) and (1+x^{20})/(1+x^4). The trailing '2' after (1+x^{20})/(1+x^4) is probably an exponent/annotation (squared), as with '|1-xx|^2'.
'-½+ε+ε^4-5/2' is uncertain; it may be a scratch evaluation related to ε+ε^4 = (√5-1)/2.

The rotated lower-left products are only partly legible. The visible exponents (1, 4, 6, 9, 11, 14, 19 and 2, 3, 7, 8, 12, 13, 17, 18) form residue classes mod 5, and the denominators are four factors (1+x).
